title: Fine wine and collecting
subtitle: Wine as an asset
objectives: Explain what makes a fine wine collectable

steps.title: What is collected
steps.body: Collectable wines age well and have a track record of price growth. Top Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne, Barolo, vintage Port and a few others dominate. The Liv-ex index tracks prices of these wines like a stock market. Only a tiny share of the world's wine, well under 1%, trades this way.
steps.highlight: A tiny share, mainly a few regions

steps.title: En primeur
steps.body: En primeur, or futures, is a way of buying Bordeaux and some other wines before they are bottled. Châteaux release a share of the wine in spring after the harvest, through négociants. Buyers pay in advance and receive bottles about two years later. The idea is to secure scarce wine at a lower price, but recent prices have often risen little after release.
steps.highlight: Pay now, receive in two years

steps.prompt: Buying Bordeaux before it is bottled is called en ____.
steps.explanation: En primeur lets buyers secure wine early, through the Bordeaux négociant system.

steps.title: Provenance and storage
steps.body: A collectable bottle's value depends on provenance: where it has been stored and by whom. Professional bonded warehouses keep wine at steady temperatures and record each movement. Wine fraud exists: the 2012 case of Rudy Kurniawan, who faked old Burgundies, showed how hard verification can be.

steps.prompt: Provenance, the record of how a bottle was stored, affects its value.
steps.explanation: Yes. Buyers pay more for wine with a clear, professional storage history.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A few regions dominate fine wine collecting
En primeur lets buyers pay early for Bordeaux
Provenance and storage protect value, and fraud exists
